It says the City sold the land without considering the need for affordable housing, and attached no conditions requiring buyers to build affordable housing. Mayor Geordin Hill-Lewis calls the case "electioneering" and says the City will oppose it. The South African Human Rights Commission (SAHRC) has accused the City of Cape Town of failing to consider the pressing need for affordable and social housing when it auctioned off 49 municipal-owned properties earlier this year. The SAHRC has applied to the Western Cape High Court for an interdict to stop any further steps in the sale and transfer of the properties until the court has reviewed the City's decisions.

Meeks, Ranking Member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and Senator Jeanne Shaheen, Ranking Member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, released the following statement on the Trump administration’s intent to terminate South Africa from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) trade program: “The Trump administration’s policy toward South Africa has prioritized political spectacle and disputed narratives over substantive diplomatic engagement and longstanding U.S. strategic interests. Trade Representative’s announcement that South Africa will soon lose its benefits under the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) risks further undermining American economic interests while handing China a strategic advantage. At a time when the United States should be encouraging manufacturers to diversify their supply chains away from China, trade preference programs like AGOA are critical tools for strengthening commercial ties with alternative markets. Rather than advancing this objective, the administration’s decision threatens to disrupt established supply chains, weaken opportunities for American manufacturers, and cede economic influence to China. “AGOA has long been a valuable tool for U.S. economic relationships across Africa that both promote African prosperity and create opportunities for American businesses.

Together, these three pillars ensure that value created from African resources remains on African soil.

stories.title: Kenyan pharmacists warn against viral craze of using allergy drug for vaginal tightening
stories.summary: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Cetirizine is commonly used to relieve allergy symptoms By Wycliffe Muia Reporting from Nairobi Published 2 hours ago Kenyan pharmacists have warned women against inserting allergy tablets into their vaginas in an attempt to make them tighter, following the spread of potentially dangerous medical advice on social media. The warning follows a wave of social media posts promoting cetirizine - a widely available oral antihistamine used to treat allergies - as a way of tightening the vagina, supposedly to enhance sexual pleasure. Although antihistamines can sometimes cause dryness as a side effect, experts say this does not strengthen vaginal muscles. "Dryness is not tightness... instead, it may increase friction, discomfort, and the risk of tissue injury," the Pharmaceutical Society of Kenya (PSK) said. "Inserting oral tablets is unsafe. Cetirizine tablets are made to be swallowed. Their ingredients have not been tested on delicate vaginal tissue," it added.

According to IOM latest report, the displaced victims correspond to 316 households across the districts of Mocímboa da Praia, Macomia, Muidumbe, and Meluco. The displaced population includes 265 men, 386 women, and 584 children. The IOM also identified 87 pregnant women, 58 elderly individuals (over 60 years old), 18 people with disabilities, and four children who are unaccompanied or separated from their families. Kenya suffers corruption at every level of society - from endless petty bribes paid to traffic police, to vast procurement scandals that go to the top of government, and it has contributed to massive protests over the past two years. The World Bank report said the east African country is among the most corrupt of its peers among lower middle-income countries, and estimates that the governance weaknesses are adding around 370 billion shillings (€2.4 billion) every year to Kenya 's fiscal deficit, equivalent to two percent of GDP. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines This figure, which its authors describe as "conservative", comes from lost taxes, inefficient public spending, higher borrowing costs, and other issues caused by corruption . stories.title: UK commits to 'time-bound' talks on slavery apology
stories.summary: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Andy Burnham has ruled out reparations but is open to a formal apology By Chris Mason Political editor Published 5 November 2026, 02:17 GMT The UK has signed up to "structured, time-bound, inclusive and good-faith" talks that address the "historical harms" of the transatlantic slave trade, Commonwealth leaders in Antigua have said. The formal conclusions marking the end of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, known as the communique, is the joint text setting out what has been agreed. The 18 page document , external includes a paragraph in which the leaders "welcome the agreement of the Government of the United Kingdom to engage in a structured, time-bound, inclusive and good-faith dialogue with affected parties addressing the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans and its historical harms". It comes after Prime Minister Andy Burnham opened the door to a formal apology on behalf of the UK for its role in the slave trade, while ruling out the prospect of reparations. Officials said the timeframe for the talks would be agreed at a later date, though the Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has suggested they are likely to conclude in around a year.

stories.title: Why a US-funded vaccine trial on babies was cancelled in Guinea-Bissau

The trial was funded by the US, under Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, who has a long record of expressing scepticism about vaccines. Police have seized a batch of vaccines from the research centre at the heart of the controversy. The proposed trial drew international criticism because it planned to withhold a vaccine recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) from half of the participating newborns. Some public health experts argued that the proposed trial raised broader questions about whether vulnerable populations in African countries were being asked to take risks that researchers would not accept in wealthier countries.

The recommendation marks the first time vaccines specifically designed to protect against Bundibugyo virus, the virus responsible for the current outbreak, will be evaluated during an outbreak of the disease. The two vaccine candidates are ChAdOx1, developed by the University of Oxford with the Serum Institute of India, and Moderna's mRNA-1469. WHO's independent Technical Advisory Group on Candidate Vaccine Prioritization recommended both for further clinical evaluation this week, based on available preclinical and early clinical evidence. The companies were informed on Monday.

stories.title: Can an African feminist have a white wedding? It’s complicated | Patience Akumu
stories.summary: Patience and Mark at their wedding. ‘Getting married as an African feminist felt like the pope renouncing Catholicism – uncomfortable and unlikely.’ Photograph: Courtesy of Patience Akumu View image in fullscreen Patience and Mark at their wedding. ‘Getting married as an African feminist felt like the pope renouncing Catholicism – uncomfortable and unlikely.’ Photograph: Courtesy of Patience Akumu Can an African feminist have a white wedding? It’s complicated Patience Akumu I wanted to be a beacon of black feminist love; my friends and family teased me for being a sellout W e had been together 20 years, had two children and had a customary marriage with our village sub-county two years ago without any real plans for a church wedding. So we called our second ceremony a celebration of love and not a wedding. How else would a self-professed African feminist survive being the centre of a colonial and Abrahamic religious ceremony that also manages to reinforce the most male-centred aspects of African culture? Our invitations came directly from me and my partner Mark, not – as is traditional – from our families, and in the form of a playful gif featuring the song Love Potion from the South African group Mafikizolo, a reminder that this was a wedding on our terms.

stories.summary: L'exclusion de l'Afrique du Sud de l'accord de l'Agoa aura «un impact a priori assez limité» La première confédération syndicale d’Afrique du Sud a exhorté ce 3 novembre 2026 son gouvernement à poursuivre ses discussions avec Washington pour sauver un accord commercial (Agoa) avec les États-Unis dont dépendent des centaines d'emplois, dans certains secteurs comme l’industrie viticole ou encore les producteurs d’agrumes. « S'il y a des effets négatifs sur certaines filières sud-africaines, comme notamment le secteur automobile, au niveau macroéconomique, l'impact a priori sera assez limité », estime toutefois un expert. stories.title: Suited and booted: How Joseph Kabila went from president to rebel leader
stories.summary: Image source, Getty By Ondiro Oganga Published 31 October 2026 Joseph Kabila was a commander in the rebel alliance that brought his father to power in the Democratic Republic of Congo in 1997, went on to succeed him as president and now, at the age of 55, he is a rebel leader once again. In an even stranger twist, the man he has sworn to topple is the very man he handed power to after 18 years at the helm, and with whom he had formed a coalition government after stepping down. While one of the rebel groups he had fought against as president is part of his new alliance. His career reflects the ever-shifting nature of politics in DR Congo, where alliances are ephemeral, with the use of force a constant threat. When Kabila was named leader of the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), earlier this month, it confirmed what many Congolese had long believed â that the former president was working with the M23 rebels, who last year seized much of eastern DR Congo, including the region's main cities of Goma and Bukavu.

stories.title: Roy Moxham obituary
stories.summary: Roy Moxham visited India many times, partly to carry out research for his books View image in fullscreen Roy Moxham visited India many times, partly to carry out research for his books Obituary Roy Moxham obituary My uncle Roy Moxham, who has died aged 86, was a former tea plantation supervisor who in later life turned his hand to writing about tea and about India , a country he visited many times on extended trips. His most successful book was The Great Hedge of India (2001), which was published not just in English but in multiple Indian languages. The hedge of the title, which was four metres high and 2.5m wide, was made of thorny shrubs and stretched 2,500 miles across British India to form a customs line guarded by 12,000 men on behalf of the East India Company. Following independence in 1947 it all but disappeared, but Roy spent many of his visits to the country looking for vestiges, eventually finding a small surviving section. He cut a branch from it, and it is now in the possession of his brother John (my father), kept safely in his study.

stories.title: Refugee athlete to make history for second time at Youth Olympics
stories.summary: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Yiech Pur Biel (left) is leading the first ever refugee team at the Youth Olympics By Lizzy Bella BBC Newsbeat Published 30 October 2026 When he started running, Yiech Pur Biel had to compete barefoot. Far from home in a new country, it was the first step towards rebuilding his life as a refugee. "That's when I decided now it is time to depend on myself and also to start a new life with determination," he tells BBC Newsbeat. In 2016, Biel made history competing in the 800m event as part of the first Olympic refugee team at the Rio summer Olympics in Brazil. Ten years on, he's making history again leading the first refugee team for the Youth Olympics as their Chef de Mission. Joining almost 3,000 athletes, the small team of six will be wanting to make sure their debut counts - but Biel says they're also hoping to send a message that "refugees still need our help".

stories.title: How Kenyans got caught in $130m US ghost student scam
stories.summary: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, US Assistant Attorney General Colin M McDonald vowed to pursue all those involved By Ondiro Oganga Reporting from Nairobi Published 30 October 2026 In May 2024, Francis Mogambi arrived in the United States after winning the Diversity Visa lottery, a programme that gives people from around the world a chance to become permanent residents. Just over two years later, the Kenyan national found himself at the centre of a US investigation into an alleged nationwide scheme to defraud the federal student aid system. On 19 October 2026, a grand jury in Nebraska indicted Mogambi on five counts of theft of government money and five counts of aggravated identity theft. Prosecutors allege that, between November 2025 and May 2026, he worked with associates in Kenya to steal the identities of US citizens and use them to fraudulently enroll fictitious students in American colleges. Once the fake students were enrolled, Mogambi allegedly diverted their financial aid payments to himself, keeping 30% and sending the remainder to his associates in Kenya.

stories.title: Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg
stories.summary: Wemmer Pan Road, near Rosettenville in Johannesburg, has been occupied by illegal gold miners. Photograph: James Oatway/The Guardian There is no end in sight for the drivers of illegal mining, while police action appears ineffective By Rachel Savage in Durban Deep C ora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since she first started treating injured animals in the townships around Roodepoort, west of Johannesburg, in 1991. But as the price of gold has soared, so too has activity in the abandoned mine shafts that mark the area. In late September, dozens of zama zamas – the name given to illegal miners in South Africa , meaning roughly “to take a chance” in Zulu – arrived to dig for gold across the dirt road from her charity, Claw (Community Led Animal Welfare). Soon, they were taking water for their panning and processing from the organisation’s two 25,000-litre water tanks, which are filled irregularly by the city government for the 100 or so rescued and injured animals on site. “We’ve asked them really nicely and haven’t ever refused them water to drink … But, for the first time ever, we closed the gate at 12 [midday], because we literally had about two buckets of water left,” Bailey said in mid-October.
